rv.q: "The Visit" is a haunting, haunted knot of Expressionist storytelling, a masterly 100-minute powerhouse with liltingly gruesome songs that create their own macabre world unlike anything onstage in recent memory.
“The Visit” is sophisticated and beautiful and yet has that typical glorious chilling view of man that you expect from a Kander and Ebb show.
This production, previously seen last summer at the Williamstown Theatre Festival, was worth the wait.
This show most assuredly deserves to be here, if feeling, music and craft are the perennial guideposts.
It’s hard to think of a better sync between role and star.
It has a dark, sinister beauty — and who could resist a visit from Chita?
If 'The Visit' occupies a sort of landscaped plateau in this terrain, its leading lady continues to tower.
Rivera, at 82, remains a magnetic stage presence, investing Claire with both steely determination and surprising vulnerability.
But D’Amour, while clearly sympathetic to her characters, conjures a world too neatly balanced, too eccentric, too oddly wholesome.
But unquestionably, the reason to see The Visit even with its flaws is the star, whose brittle vocals cut like ice.
But as long as it has taken to get here, The Visit still hasn’t quite arrived.
It remains fascinating and alluring, if finally repetitive and frustrating.
The Visit has been fourteen years in the making.
This brilliant musical is a James Ensor painting drained of most colors, and the mix of John Kander's riffs and plaintive ballads suit that dark vision to perfection.
Rivera’s vital performance as Claire Zacahanassian, a woman who has married both well and often, is just one reason “The Visit” is notable, here at the end of a crowded theater season.
It's a Visit no musical theater lover will want to miss.
Her presence alone makes The Visit worth the trip.
Filled with mordant humor and haunting melodies, it depicts a grim Brecht/Weill world of misery and corruption.
However, all that veteran talent yields decidedly mixed results.
Yet despite its shortcomings, it's intriguing to see Kander and Ebb create this world, an odd dystopia where a kickline and jazz hands have their place.
Wildcat? No. Claire and "The Visit" are too domesticated for their own good.
Although it makes for a provocative thriller, the score is weak, dreary and derivative of Kander and Ebb’s earlier work.
This is a show that should be laid to rest.
For fans of Rivera, this production is simply unmissable.
A passionate heart beats inside 'The Visit,' for all its formal innovation and chilly beauty.
However, persistently, this is an underwhelming group of songs that never rises to the heights the duo has so consistently delivered in the past.

tn.cat: Best Lighting Design of a Musical

cn.t: Critics praise Chita Rivera's magnetic performance in this dark Kander and Ebb musical, but find the show itself a mixed bag—admiring its austere design and somber themes while noting it lacks warmth and commercial appeal.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
